stories.title: CUEA: Catholic Educators Urged to Build on Youths’ Return to Faith Through Music
stories.description:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
Catholic school heads across Kenya have been challenged to seize the growing wave of young people expressing their faith through music and social media as a foundation for deepening Catholic education in schools.
Addressing head teachers at their annual meeting at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA), under their umbrella body, Catholic Primary Schools Heads Association – Kenya (CaPSHA-K), the university's Deputy Vice Chancellor for Academic and Student Affairs, Prof. Justus M. Munyoki, noted that many young people in the Catholic Church in Kenya have been taking to the streets to “sing Catholic hymns and posting videos of themselves in church singing for the Lord.”
Sharing the welcome message on behalf of the outgoing Vice Chancellor, Very Rev. Prof. Stephen Mbungua Ngari, at the capacity-building conference on Tuesday, August 18, the Deputy Vice Chancellor for Academic and Student Affairs said that this trend is “a clear sign that the youth are returning to and embracing the Church in their own way.”
He called on the teachers and school heads to take advantage of this phenomenon to reinforce the philosophy of Catholic education, rather than let the moment pass unused.
Reflecting on the theme of the 2026 conference, Catholic Schools: Rooted in Faith, Rising with Purpose, Prof. Munyoki referenced the Book of Hebrews 11:1, which describes faith as “confidence in what is hoped for and assurance about what is not seen.”
He posed a challenge to head teachers to examine whether their schools promote genuine confidence that pupils would succeed in life, and whether pupils themselves held onto hope for a good outcome from their studies.
He acknowledged the difficult realities many school heads face, including low funding, uncooperative parents, and indiscipline, and encouraged them to remain focused and to keep rising with purpose by achieving progress one step at a time.
Prof. Munyoki shared on Pope Leo XIV's Apostolic Letter, Drawing New Maps of Hope, which describes educational charisms not as fixed formulas but as living responses to the needs of every age, and presents Catholic schools as communities where faith, culture, and life come together in harmony.
He asked teachers to view their schools through this lens, forming the whole person and nurturing pupils' ability to pursue knowledge in ways that speak to their own hopes for the future.
According to Prof. Munyoki, CUEA stands as an international Catholic institution, with over 35 nationalities drawn from across the Eastern Africa region and beyond, and with more than 32,000 alumni. He reaffirmed CUEA's continued support for the Commission of Education and the wider Catholic education sector.

stories.title: SOUTH SUDAN: Cardinal Challenges New Priests to Promote Peace
stories.description:
By: Ginaba Lino
South Sudan’s Cardinal has challenged newly ordained priests to reflect on their priesthood, embrace obedience, and make their ministry a source of healing and transformation for communities affected by conflict and division. Cardinal Stephen Ameyu Martin Mulla made the call on Saturday, August 15, during the ordination of three new priests, urging them to remain faithful to Christ and understand priesthood as a vocation of service rather than a position of privilege or status.
He said the Church’s contribution to peace and reconciliation depends largely on the commitment of her clergy to serve faithfully and accompany the people entrusted to their care.“If these people today are still in war, it is because we clergymen have gone wrong,” Cardinal Ameyu said, challenging priests to examine whether they are faithfully carrying out the mission entrusted to them by Christ.
He urged the newly ordained priests to faithfully administer the sacraments, particularly the Sacrament of Reconciliation, which he described as an important instrument for renewing both priests and the people of God.The Cardinal said priests must become examples of forgiveness if they are to help communities overcome hatred, division and conflict.
“We have not administered the proper sacrament,” he said, emphasizing that priests have been given the responsibility and capacity to forgive as ministers of God’s mercy.
Cardinal Ameyu urged the new priests to baptize and confirm Christians, witness marriages and remain attentive to people in need of God’s mercy.
“What you have accepted today is a very difficult task,” he told the priests, stressing that their vocation requires perseverance, spiritual discipline and a close relationship with Jesus Christ.
He encouraged them to remain united with Jesus, the Church and their bishops, describing obedience in love as an essential foundation of priestly ministry.
“Without obedience there is no church. Without obedience there is no family. Without obedience there is no institution,” he said.
The Cardinal also challenged religious men and women to understand their vows as a call to become instruments of God’s salvation among His people, rather than commitments limited to their respective communities.
He placed humility at the centre of priestly formation, warning that priests cannot effectively serve the people of God without recognizing their dependence on God’s mercy.
“Unless you are formed as humble human beings, we cannot become good priests in the future,” he said.
Cardinal Ameyu encouraged priests to begin each day in prayer, kneeling before Christ and acknowledging their need for forgiveness, guidance and renewal.
He linked this call to humility to the example of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose Assumption into Heaven was celebrated during the occasion.
Reflecting on the Gospel of the day, he highlighted Mary’s visitation to Elizabeth as an example of humility and service, saying her response to God’s call was expressed through reaching out to another person.
The Cardinal said Mary’s example reminds Christians that responding to God should lead to service and solidarity rather than self-importance.
He further explained that the Assumption of Mary, body and soul, points to the Christian hope of resurrection and humanity’s ultimate destiny with God.
Cardinal Ameyo urged the faithful to rise above divisions created by tribe, nationality, tradition and other human identities, emphasizing the common belonging of all people to God.
He challenged the priests to regularly examine their lives and ministry, warning against self-praise, pride and attitudes that could distance them from the people they are called to serve.
The Cardinal said the priesthood must never become a source of personal privilege, but must remain a ministry of service rooted in humility of Christ.
He also called on the faithful to support their priests through prayer, encouragement, and constructive correction.
“It is your duty, as the people of God, to correct these people who are up here at the altar. It is your duty to pray for them,” he said.
The Metropolitan Archbishop of Juba Archdiocese stressed that priests need the prayers of the faithful despite their own commitment to prayer and the celebration of Mass.
He further encouraged priests to remain honest about their vocation and to make responsible decisions if they discover that they are no longer able or willing to serve the people of God, and warned against distractions and behaviors that undermine priestly ministry, urging priests to remain united, disciplined, prayerful, and willing to seek forgiveness and renewal.
The Cardinal concluded by calling for a Church rooted in forgiveness, unity, charity and faith, expressing confidence that God would continue to guide His Church through difficult times.
